summary.text: Earth's energy budget is the balance between the energy Earth receives from the Sun and the energy it loses back to space.
When incoming and outgoing energy match, the climate stays relatively stable, but when more comes in than goes out the planet warms.
Human-caused changes to the makeup of the atmosphere have driven a warming imbalance that averaged about 460 TW from 2005 to 2019.

facts.label: Average sunlight arriving
facts.value: About 340 W/m², a quarter of the solar constant

facts.label: Heat from Earth's interior
facts.value: About 47 TW, 0.027% of the surface budget

items.prompt: Sunlight hits Earth face-on like light on a disk, yet the average over the whole planet is only a quarter of that intensity. Why a quarter?

options.label: Clouds turn back three quarters of all sunlight
A sphere has four times the area of its disk
The Sun only shines on Earth one hour in four
The air absorbs three quarters before the ground

items.explain: A sphere's surface area is four times its cross-sectional area, so the global yearly average at the top of the atmosphere is one quarter of the solar constant.

items.prompt: Greenhouse gases in the air suddenly increase. What happens first to the heat Earth sends out to space?

options.label: It rises, so Earth cools down quickly
It stays exactly the same as before
It drops, leaving a warming imbalance
It switches from infrared to visible light

items.explain: More heat trapping by greenhouse gases forces a decrease in outgoing longwave radiation and a warming energy imbalance.

items.prompt: Earth's interior leaks heat from radioactive decay and from the planet's formation. How big is that next to the energy from sunlight?

options.label: Far less than one percent
Roughly one tenth
Roughly one third
About the same amount

items.explain: Geothermal heat is about 47 TW, only 0.027% of the surface energy budget, dwarfed by 173000 TW of incoming sunlight.

items.prompt: Earth starts taking in more energy than it gives off. Why does the global surface temperature not jump right away?

options.label: Clouds instantly reflect the extra energy
The extra energy is lost through Earth's core
Thermometers only update once each decade
Oceans, land and ice take time to warm up

items.explain: Changes in the energy budget take time to show up in surface temperature because of the thermal inertia of the oceans, land and cryosphere.

items.prompt: Sunlight soaked up by the ground eventually leaves Earth. In what form does that energy finally go out to space?

options.label: As visible light, like a glow
As longwave radiation
As warm air drifting off
As water vapour escaping

items.explain: Absorbed solar energy becomes heat, moves up by various routes, and ultimately all outgoing energy is radiated into space as longwave radiation.

items.prompt: The Sun heats the tropics more than the poles. What does the planet's push to even out that energy produce?

options.label: A steady drain of heat into the deep crust
A pause in the Earth's daily rotation
Earth's climate, through air, water, ice and life
Earth's magnetic field, through moving charges

items.explain: Uneven heating sends energy toward equilibrium, which drives interactions among water, ice, air, rock and living things, and the result is Earth's climate.
